clinicalPearls: Movement disorders are classified as hypokinetic (poverty of movement, e.g. parkinsonism with rest tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia) versus hyperkinetic (excess movement, e.g. chorea, dystonia, tremor); the rest tremor and cogwheel rigidity of Parkinson's disease are extrapyramidal signs distinct from the action tremor of essential tremor (Harrison 22e p.3508; cf. p.197 ch.31).

Essential tremor is an action/postural tremor; a key pitfall is mislabeling it as Parkinson's disease, but Parkinson tremor is characteristically a rest tremor accompanied by cogwheel rigidity and bradykinesia, whereas essential tremor lacks these and worsens with sustained posture or movement (Harrison 22e p.3508).

Huntington's disease is an autosomal dominant degenerative disorder producing the triad of chorea, psychiatric/behavioral disturbance (mood, anxiety, psychosis), and progressive dementia; the unpredictable choreic movements give the gait a characteristic dancing quality (Harrison 22e p.3508; gait described p.~3535 ch.32; HD as autosomal-dominant dementia p.198 ch.31).

Dystonia is defined as sustained muscle contractions producing repetitive twisting movements and abnormal posture; it often has a genetic basis, but new asymmetric dystonia—particularly involving gait—in a younger adult may be an early sign of Parkinson's disease (Harrison 22e p.3508; cf. gait chapter p.~3535).

Sydenham's chorea (a manifestation of acute rheumatic fever after group A streptococcal infection) is the prototypical post-infectious chorea: it occurs mainly in females after a prolonged latent period, affects especially the head (darting tongue movements) and upper limbs, may be generalized or hemichoreic, and is frequently accompanied by emotional lability or obsessive-compulsive traits; >50% of patients presenting with chorea have carditis, so echocardiography is warranted (Harrison 22e p.3508; ch. on rheumatic fever p.~2992).

Tardive dyskinesia is a drug-induced hyperkinetic disorder seen with chronic exposure to antipsychotics and other agents that block the D2 dopamine receptor, and is a common cause of stereotypic movement and gait disturbances (Harrison 22e p.3508).
harrison.pathophysiology: Movement disorders arise predominantly from dysfunction of the basal ganglia (striatum = caudate plus putamen) and their cortical and thalamic connections, which modulate motor output rather than directly generating it; disruption of these circuits yields either hypokinetic syndromes (parkinsonism) or hyperkinetic syndromes (chorea, dystonia, tremor). Huntington's disease is caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat (autosomal dominant) with degeneration of the striatum. Wilson's disease results from impaired copper excretion with copper accumulation in liver and brain. Tardive dyskinesia reflects chronic blockade of striatal D2 dopamine receptors (Harrison 22e p.3508; basal ganglia/striatum anatomy p.~199-200 ch.31).
additionalDifferentials: Parkinson's disease (rest tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia) — see parkinsons_disease
Progressive supranuclear palsy (axial rigidity, vertical gaze palsy, early falls)
Multiple-system atrophy and corticobasal syndrome (asymmetric akinesia, rigidity, dystonia, myoclonus, alien limb)
Orthostatic tremor (high-frequency low-amplitude leg tremor, shakiness on standing relieved by sitting/walking)
infectionMimics: Sydenham's chorea following group A streptococcal infection (acute rheumatic fever)
Other post-infectious or autoimmune (paraneoplastic) chorea and movement disorders
nonInfectiousMimics: Wilson's disease (copper accumulation; young patient with chorea, dystonia, parkinsonism or tremor)
Drug-induced movements from dopamine-receptor blockers (tardive dyskinesia, acute dystonia)
additionalInvestigations: Genetic testing for the CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion when Huntington's disease is suspected

Serum ceruloplasmin (low), 24-h urinary copper (elevated), slit-lamp exam for Kayser-Fleischer rings, and liver copper to evaluate for Wilson's disease in any young patient with unexplained chorea, dystonia, tremor or parkinsonism
Echocardiography when chorea suggests acute rheumatic fever (>50% have carditis); anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase B titers for preceding streptococcal infection
MRI brain to assess for basal ganglia and other structural/degenerative changes
redFlags: New chorea, dystonia, tremor or parkinsonism in an adolescent or young adult — exclude Wilson's disease (treatable; look for Kayser-Fleischer rings, low ceruloplasmin, high urinary copper) before manifestations become irreversible
Chorea with autosomal dominant family history plus psychiatric change and cognitive decline — consider Huntington's disease
Acute chorea (especially in a young female) — evaluate for acute rheumatic fever and carditis with echocardiography
Abnormal movements in a patient on long-term antipsychotics/D2 blockers — recognize tardive dyskinesia and acute dystonic reactions
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis is disorder-specific. Essential tremor is typically slowly progressive and non-degenerative. Huntington's disease is relentlessly progressive and degenerative. Wilson's disease can improve substantially with prompt diagnosis and copper-chelating treatment before end-stage manifestations become irreversible. Sydenham's chorea is usually self-limited, with choreiform movements resolving within about 6 weeks, occasionally up to 6 months, though associated obsessive-compulsive or emotional symptoms may persist longer (Harrison 22e p.3508; Wilson p.~2713 ch.355; chorea p.~2992).
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing essential (action) tremor as Parkinson's disease, or vice versa — Parkinson tremor is a rest tremor with cogwheel rigidity and bradykinesia
Failing to test for Wilson's disease in a young patient with new movement disorder; Wilson's may present with chronic hepatitis long before neurologic signs or Kayser-Fleischer rings appear
Overlooking carditis in a patient presenting with chorea (Sydenham's), since chorea may be the sole or delayed manifestation of rheumatic fever
Not recognizing drug-induced/tardive movements from D2-blocking medications
harrison.severityClassification: No single unified severity scale spans all movement disorders; assessment is disorder-specific and functional. Chorea, for example, ranges from movements evident only on careful examination in mild cases to inability to perform activities of daily living in severe cases (Harrison 22e p.3508).
